exercise.name: V-up

reference.title: V-up (male)
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

exercise.mechanics: Compound (trunk flexion and hip flexion together)

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you fold up, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1.2 s up, short balance, about 2 s down

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief balance, 2 s down
prescription.progression: Tuck-up first, then V-up, then a slower lowering or a hold at the top (V-sit)

cues.text: Lie flat, legs straight and together, arms straight overhead on the mat.
Breathe out and lift the arms and legs together, folding at the hips.
Balance on the hips with the hands reaching toward the shins; chest lifted, legs straight.
Breathe in and lower both ends slowly; keep the low back from arching as the legs come down.
Touch down lightly, arms overhead, and go again.

mistakes.mistake: Arms reach but legs stay low (or the reverse)
mistakes.fix: Lift both ends at the same time so they meet over the hips.
Lower in about 2 s; stop just above the mat if you can.

mistakes.mistake: Low back arching off the mat as the legs lower
mistakes.fix: Brace and shorten the range, or bend the knees (tuck-up).
Squeeze the thighs together and keep the knees soft but long.

kinematics.measure: Trunk (pelvis to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Trunk and legs meet over the hips; no study defines the angles (clinical opinion)
Legs straight, rising to meet the hands (clinical opinion)
Deep hip flexion at the top: the V (clinical opinion)
Upper back curls, chest stays fairly long (clinical opinion)
From overhead on the mat to reaching toward the shins (clinical opinion)
About 1 s up, 2 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Andersson, Nilsson, Ma and Thorstensson 1997, abdominal and hip flexor muscle activation during various training exercises (Eur J Appl Physiol 75:115-123; PMID 9118976)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)
Escamilla et al. 2006, electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises (Phys Ther 86(5):656-671)
Axler and McGill 1997, low-back loads over a variety of abdominal exercises: searching for the safest abdominal challenge (Med Sci Sports Exerc 29(6):804-811)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
Advanced: it combines a sit-up and a straight-leg raise, the two higher-compression options in McGill's comparison (McGill 1998).

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion or straight-leg work.
modify: Bend the knees (tuck-up) or lift one leg at a time.
Shorten the range: hands to the knees.
progressions: Light weight held in the hands.

muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis curls the trunk and holds the pelvis while the legs rise. No study measured the V-up itself; it joins a sit-up and a bilateral leg raise, and bilateral (not unilateral) leg lifts needed abdominal activation (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Iliopsoas lifts the legs and the trunk at the same time: hip flexors were highly active in exercises that flex the hip by lifting either the upper body or the legs (Andersson 1997), and leg raises gave the highest psoas activity in McGill's data (McGill 1998).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Iliopsoas lifts the legs and the trunk at the same time: hip flexors were highly active in exercises that flex the hip by lifting either the upper body or the legs (Andersson 1997), and leg raises gave the highest psoas activity in McGill's data (McGill 1998).
muscleNotes.obliques_r: Assist trunk flexion and keep the balance on the hips steady.
muscleNotes.obliques_l: Assist trunk flexion and keep the balance on the hips steady.
muscleNotes.quads_r: Rectus femoris flexes the hips and keeps the knees straight; rectus femoris activity was higher in hip-flexion sit-ups than in leg lifts (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.quads_l: Rectus femoris flexes the hips and keeps the knees straight; rectus femoris activity was higher in hip-flexion sit-ups than in leg lifts (Andersson 1997).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Keep the legs pressed together (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Keep the legs pressed together (clinical opinion).
